summary: Ephemeral driver IO attach lag causing reserved-pool throughput sag
description:
Issue summary:
An intermittent surge of host-level IO activity (short-lived bursts from a background checkpoint writer) is causing large GPU attach/handshake latencies in a reserved pool. The attach delays lead to the autoscaler and scheduler seeing transient capacity unavailability, which triggers rapid slot reassignments and an observable throughput sag for the customer's reserved capacity window.

Impact:
- Streamline AI reports elevated p95/p99 latency for batched requests during a 30-90s window several times per hour.
- Throughput drop: observed 20-40% drop in steady-state token throughput for the affected partition during bursts.
- Application-level errors: a small percentage (~0.2%) of requests return 5xx attach-timeouts before autoscaler fallback kicks in.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: reserved-cluster-14 (prod-us-west)
- Host type: 8x A100 (mainly homogeneous) with local NVMe used for checkpointing
- Agent/runtime: serving-runtime v2.3.8, driver-manager v1.9.1
- Observed windows: recurring between 09:40–16:20 UTC on 2026-03-10/11/12

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Customer workload triggers periodic small checkpoint writes on host local NVMe (background writer every ~10–15m).
2) Within 10–30s of the write spike, host IO saturation causes elevated kernel scheduling and occasionally delayed driver attach handshakes reported by driver-manager.
3) Scheduler marks GPUs as slow-to-attach; autoscaler initiates ephemeral reassignments/fallbacks to maintain latency SLOs.
4) Result is temporary slot churn, increased p99 latency, and drop in overall served tokens until KV caches and prewarmed contexts repopulate.

Observed logs & metrics pointers:
- Grafana: /d/dedicated/pool-14/attach-latency (panel shows 10–40s attach spikes)
- Cloudwatch host IO spike metric: host-io.iops spike to 150k for 20–60s (normal ~12k)
- driver-manager log excerpt (see logs field below)

Notes: pattern is repeatable on production under the same customer traffic profile; isolated to reserved pool nodes where local NVMe checkpoint daemon is enabled.
investigation_notes:
Timeline and hypotheses: 2026-03-10 10:05 UTC first customer alert. Initial hypothesis: noisy-tenant CPU/GPU contention. After correlating kernel and driver logs we observed a different pattern — short-lived host NVMe IO bursts (checkpoint writer) correlate precisely with attach-handshake latency and occasional nvme timeouts. Key findings:
- driver-manager reports delayed attach ACKs tied to increased host iowait (iowait > 60% during spikes).
- Autoscaler sees slot unavailability and triggers reactive switching causing slot fragmentation.
- Reproduced in staging by enabling synthetic checkpoint writer and firing small bursts; attach latency reproducible.
Potential root cause: host-level IO jitter causes driver handshake/backoff loops to extend, making GPUs briefly unavailable to scheduler. This is perceived as GPU shortage and triggers thrash.
Next steps: 1) apply mitigation to reserved pool to rate-limit checkpoint writer; 2) add driver-manager timeout backoff improvements to reduce sensitivity to brief IO noise; 3) schedule follow-up to modify node-local checkpointing schedule and evaluate NVMe QoS settings.

resolution_notes:
Mitigations applied (temporary):
- Throttled the customer background checkpoint writer via host-level systemd timer adjustments on reserved-cluster-14.
- Enabled prewarm persistence for the customer's most-used routes to maintain KV cache across short attach latencies.
- Implemented a temporary autoscaler soft-fail threshold to avoid immediate slot churn for attach latencies under 30s.
Planned permanent actions:
- Merge driver-manager PR to smooth attach backoff and avoid aggressive reassignments (PR linked above).
- Run NVMe QoS experiment to cap checkpoint IO bursts and update reserved pool runbook to recommend IO limits on hosts with local checkpointing.
- Postmortem and runbook update scheduled after staging validation.
workaround: Customer-level workaround applied: reduced checkpoint frequency to every 60m and applied a 5s jitter; Redwood applied prewarm persistence. These steps reduced attach-timing events by ~90% during observation window.
